title: Ownship Maneuvers Improve the Solution
summary: Learn why changing your own course or speed creates better geometry for solving a contact's track.
objectives: Recognize when initial bearing data creates ambiguous solutions
Observe how an ownship maneuver changes the bearing pattern
Understand the difference between good and bad crossing geometry
Submit a stable course estimate after a maneuver

tasks.title: Initial Ambiguity
tasks.description: The contact is on bearing 330° and appears to be steady. Without an estimate, predict: could this contact be on a course of 090° or 180°? Why might both be possible with only one bearing line?

tasks.title: Observe the Maneuver Effect
tasks.description: Step forward past T+2:00 when the ownship turns east. Watch how the bearing rate changes. Does it get faster or slower after the turn? What does that reveal about the contact's true course?

tasks.title: Submit Estimate
tasks.description: After observing the bearing history through the maneuver, submit your best estimate for the contact's range, course, and speed.

hints.text: With only one bearing, the contact could be anywhere along that line at any range. A steady bearing suggests the contact and ownship are on parallel courses OR moving directly toward/away from each other.
A large change in bearing rate after a maneuver breaks the ambiguity. If the contact is crossing your bow, a turn toward it will make the bearing shift faster.
The maneuver acts as a second observation point. Compare the bearing BEFORE the turn to the bearing AFTER the turn to triangulate.

debriefRules.feedback: Notice how the maneuver at 2:00 made the contact's course much clearer. Before the turn, the bearing drift was too slow to distinguish a bow-on target from a crossing one.
The ownship turn creates a triangulation baseline. The longer you wait after the turn before estimating, the better your range will be.
